paragraphs: The “Red Death” had ravaged the country for a long time. No plague had ever been so deadly or so hideous. Blood was its embodiment and its seal—the redness and horror of blood. It brought sharp pains and sudden dizziness, then heavy bleeding through the pores, followed by death. Scarlet stains on the victim’s body, especially the face, marked him as infected and shut him off from the help and sympathy of other people. The disease’s entire course, from its first attack to its end, took half an hour.

But Prince Prospero was happy, fearless and shrewd. When his lands had lost half their people, he summoned a thousand healthy, cheerful friends from among the knights and ladies of his court. With them, he withdrew into the deep seclusion of one of his fortified abbeys. This was a vast, magnificent building, created according to the prince’s own eccentric yet majestic taste. A strong, high wall surrounded it, with gates of iron. Once inside, the courtiers brought furnaces and heavy hammers and welded the bolts shut. They were determined that no sudden fit of despair or frenzy within should leave a way in or out. The abbey was well stocked with provisions. With these precautions, the courtiers could defy infection. The outside world could take care of itself. Meanwhile, it was foolish to grieve or think. The prince had supplied every means of pleasure. There were jesters. There were poets who improvised their verses. There were ballet dancers. There were musicians. There was Beauty. There was wine. All these, and safety, were inside. Outside was the “Red Death.”

Near the end of the fifth or sixth month of his seclusion, while the plague raged outside with its greatest fury, Prince Prospero entertained his thousand friends at a masked ball of extraordinary splendour.

The masquerade was a scene of sensual luxury. But first let me describe the rooms where it took place. There were seven, forming an imperial suite. In many palaces, such rooms run in a long, straight line. Their folding doors slide back almost to the walls on either side, leaving a nearly uninterrupted view through the whole suite. Here it was very different, as one might expect from the duke’s love of the bizarre. The rooms were arranged so irregularly that one could see little more than one at a time. Every twenty or thirty yards there was a sharp turn, and a new effect at each turn. On the right and left, in the centre of each wall, a tall, narrow Gothic window looked onto an enclosed corridor that followed the suite’s twists. The windows were stained glass, coloured to match the main colour of the room’s decorations. The room at the eastern end, for example, was hung in blue, and its windows were vividly blue. The second room had purple ornaments and tapestries, and purple panes. The third was green throughout, including its windows. The fourth was furnished and lit in orange, the fifth in white, the sixth in violet. The seventh was closely draped in black velvet tapestries. They covered the ceiling, hung down the walls, and fell in heavy folds onto a carpet of the same material and colour. Only in this room did the windows fail to match the decorations. Here the panes were scarlet, a deep blood-red. Nowhere in any of the seven rooms was there a lamp or candelabrum among the many golden ornaments scattered about or hanging from the ceiling. No lamp or candle gave light within the suite. Instead, in the corridors beside the rooms, a heavy three-legged stand stood opposite each window, holding a brazier of fire. Its light streamed through the coloured glass and lit the room with a glare. This produced a multitude of gaudy, fantastic appearances. But in the western, black room, the firelight falling through the blood-coloured panes onto the dark hangings was ghastly beyond measure. It made the faces of those who entered look so wild that few guests were brave enough to set foot inside at all.

In this room, against the western wall, stood a gigantic ebony clock. Its pendulum swung back and forth with a dull, heavy, monotonous clang. Whenever the minute hand completed its circuit and the hour was due to strike, the clock’s brass lungs gave out a clear, loud, deep and intensely musical sound. But its note and emphasis were so peculiar that every hour the orchestra’s musicians felt compelled to stop briefly and listen. The waltzing dancers had to stop turning, and for a moment the whole merry company was unsettled. While the clock still chimed, the most frivolous guests grew pale, and the older, quieter ones passed their hands over their foreheads, as though lost in confused dreams or thought. But once the echoes had completely faded, light laughter spread through the gathering. The musicians looked at one another and smiled, as if at their own nervousness and foolishness. They whispered promises to each other that the next chime would not affect them in the same way. Then, after sixty minutes had passed—three thousand six hundred seconds of flying Time—the clock chimed again, and the same unease, trembling and reflection returned.

Despite all this, it was a merry, magnificent celebration. The duke’s tastes were unusual. He had a fine eye for colours and effects. He ignored the rules of mere fashion. His plans were bold and fiery, his ideas glowing with barbaric splendour. Some people would have thought him mad. His followers felt that he was not. You had to hear and see and touch him to be certain that he was not.

For this great celebration, he had largely directed the arrangement of the movable decorations in the seven rooms. His own guiding taste had also shaped the masqueraders’ appearance. You may be sure they were grotesque. There was much glare, glitter, provocative strangeness and fantasy—much of what has since been seen in “Hernani.” There were fantastically patterned figures with mismatched limbs and accessories. There were feverish inventions of the sort a madman creates. There was much beauty, much indecency, much that was bizarre, something terrible, and a good deal that might have stirred disgust. In fact, a multitude of dreams stalked back and forth through the seven rooms. And these—the dreams—twisted and turned, taking their colours from the rooms and making the orchestra’s wild music seem like an echo of their steps. Then the ebony clock in the velvet hall strikes. For a moment everything is still, everything silent except the clock’s voice. The dreams stand frozen. But the echoes die away—they have lasted only an instant—and light, half-suppressed laughter floats after them. The music swells again. The dreams come alive and twist and turn more merrily than ever, taking their colours from the many-tinted windows through which the fires on the stands cast their light. Yet now no masquerader ventures into the westernmost of the seven rooms. The night is wearing away. Redder light flows through the blood-coloured panes, and the black velvet’s darkness is appalling. To anyone whose foot touches the black carpet, the nearby ebony clock sends a muffled peal, more solemnly forceful than any heard by those enjoying the more distant pleasures of the other rooms.

Those other rooms were densely crowded, and in them the heart of life beat feverishly. The celebration whirled on until at last the clock began striking midnight. Then, as I have said, the music stopped. The waltzers stopped turning, and everything paused uneasily as before. This time, however, the bell had twelve strokes to sound. Perhaps the extra time allowed more thoughts to creep into the minds of the more reflective guests. Perhaps, too, it was this that allowed many in the crowd, before the final echoes of the last stroke had completely faded, to notice a masked figure whom no one had noticed before. Whispers of this new presence spread. At last a buzz or murmur rose from the whole company, expressing disapproval and surprise—then terror, horror and disgust.

In a gathering of phantoms such as I have described, no ordinary appearance could have caused such a sensation. In truth, the freedom allowed at that night’s masquerade was almost unlimited. But this figure had outdone Herod himself, going beyond even the prince’s vague limits of decency. There are strings in the most reckless hearts that cannot be touched without stirring emotion. Even those utterly lost souls who treat life and death alike as jokes have subjects they cannot joke about. The entire company now seemed to feel deeply that the stranger’s costume and manner showed neither wit nor propriety. The figure was tall and gaunt, wrapped from head to foot in grave clothes. The mask hiding its face so closely resembled the face of a stiffened corpse that even the closest examination would have struggled to detect the deception. The wild revellers might still have tolerated all this, even if they did not approve. But the masquerader had gone so far as to take on the appearance of the Red Death. His clothes were splashed with blood. His broad forehead, and every feature of his face, were sprinkled with the scarlet horror.

When Prince Prospero saw this ghostly image, which stalked slowly and solemnly back and forth among the waltzers as though to play its part more fully, a powerful shudder shook him. At first it seemed either terror or distaste. In the next moment, his forehead reddened with rage.

“Who dares?” he demanded hoarsely of the courtiers nearby. “Who dares insult us with this blasphemous mockery? Seize him and remove his mask, so that we may know whom to hang from the battlements at sunrise!”

Prince Prospero stood in the eastern, blue room as he spoke. His words rang loudly and clearly through all seven rooms. He was a bold, vigorous man, and the music had fallen silent at a wave of his hand.

The prince stood in the blue room, with a group of pale courtiers beside him. At first, as he spoke, they made a slight rush towards the intruder, who was also nearby and now approached him with slow, stately steps. But the whole gathering felt a nameless dread at the masquerader’s outrageous pretence, and no one reached out to seize him. Unhindered, he passed within a yard of the prince. The vast company shrank from the centres of the rooms to the walls, as if moved by a single impulse. Without interruption, and with the same solemn, measured steps he had taken from the first, he passed through the blue room into the purple, from purple to green, from green to orange, from orange to white, and from white even to violet, before anyone made a determined move to stop him. Then Prince Prospero, driven mad by rage and shame at his own momentary cowardice, rushed through the six rooms. No one followed, for deadly terror had seized them all. He held a drawn dagger high. In his headlong pursuit, he had come within three or four feet of the retreating figure when it reached the far end of the velvet room and suddenly turned to face him. There was a sharp cry. The dagger fell gleaming onto the black carpet, and immediately afterwards Prince Prospero fell onto the same carpet, stretched out in death. Then, summoning the wild courage of despair, a crowd of revellers rushed into the black room and seized the masquerader. His tall figure stood upright and motionless in the ebony clock’s shadow. They gasped in unspeakable horror when they found that the grave clothes and corpse-like mask they handled so roughly contained no solid body.

Now they recognised the presence of the Red Death. He had come like a thief in the night. One by one, the revellers fell in the blood-sprinkled halls of their celebration, each dying in the despairing posture in which he fell. The ebony clock’s life went out with that of the last reveller. The fires on the stands died. And Darkness and Decay and the Red Death ruled over everything without limit.
